Right: the clique graph has one node per clique, labeled {A,B,C}, {C,D} and {C,E,F} in the same colors, and an edge for every pair that shares a node: all three pairs share C, named on each edge, so 3 edges." width="100%"} Each maximal clique of this graph becomes a node, and two are joined when the cliques share at least one node. The clique graph shows how a network's tight groups overlap and chain together, a coarse view used in community analysis (it underlies clique percolation) and in the theory of clique graphs and intersection graphs. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new undirected graph. Each node is labeled with its clique's members, such as `"{A,B,C}"`, and stores their node IDs in the attribute `"clique"`. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The maximal cliques come from `find_cliques()`, and every pair is tested for overlap, $O(k^2 s)$ for $k$ cliques of size up to $s$. Matches NetworkX's `make_max_clique_graph` (which numbers the cliques 0, 1, ... instead of labeling them by members). ## Examples {.doc-examples} Two triangles sharing node C, plus a tail C-D: three maximal cliques, all overlapping at C: ::: {#97fbf9b7 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("C", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("F", "C"), ("C", "D")]) cg = g.clique_graph() sorted(cg.get_label_from_id(n) for n in cg.get_node_ids()), cg.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (['{A,B,C}', '{C,D}', '{C,E,F}'], 3) ``` ::: :::
